title: Enhancing Interpretability of Quantum-Assisted Blockchain Clustering via AI Agent-Based Qualitative Analysis
journal_or_venue: QAI-NLP 2025 (Proceedings of the Quantum AI and NLP Conference 2025)
abstract_summary: The paper presents a two-stage framework that combines quantitative clustering evaluation (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz) with an AI Agent-driven qualitative analysis to improve interpretability of quantum-assisted clustering on blockchain transaction data. It compares Random Quantum Features (QF) and fully trained Quantum Neural Networks (QNN), showing QNN outperforms QF on numerical metrics while the AI Agent reveals semantic differences (e.g., QNN singleton clusters), leading to a recommendation of a three-cluster configuration and a hybrid analytical strategy.
methodology_description: The paper proposes a two-stage hybrid quantum-classical methodology for clustering blockchain transaction data. Stage 1 performs quantitative evaluation: blockchain transaction records (MCO2 token on Ethereum, focusing on ten major nodes) are preprocessed (timestamp cyclical encoding, label-encoding of addresses/tokens, robust scaling of token_value and gas_price, ignoring transaction_hash) and combined with quantum-generated features to form hybrid representations. Two quantum feature strategies are compared: (1) Random Quantum Features (QF) produced by untrained/randomly initialized QNNs (Monte Carlo style) and (2) Fully Trained Quantum Neural Networks (QNN) trained end-to-end via a SwAV self-supervised loss to generate parameters for a classical feature-transformation network (Quantum-Train paradigm). Training uses the Adam optimizer with gradient clipping; the training loop applies Gaussian-noise augmentations to QNN outputs to create two views for SwAV loss. After feature extraction, K-Means clustering is applied for K in {2..6}. Clustering quality is assessed by internal metrics: Silhouette Score, Davies-Bouldin Index, and Calinski-Harabasz Index. Stage 2 uses an AI Agent (LLM-backed) for qualitative analysis: a preprocessing chain re-encodes hashed values and builds a hierarchical Clustered Information Base; an automated analytical pipeline (cluster meaning generation, intra-epoch summarization, inter-strategy comparison) produces human-readable semantic summaries and stores multi-level insights in a Knowledge Base. The AI Agent synthesizes comparisons between QF and QNN clusters (e.g., singleton/high-value clusters in QNN vs. diverse ecosystem patterns in QF) and recommends configurations (the study converges on K=3).

dataset_used: Blockchain transaction data from the MCO2 token ecosystem on Ethereum (carbon credit trading), focusing on transactions involving ten major nodes. Attributes include block_number, timestamp, from_address, to_address, token_name, token_symbol, token_value, gas_price, and transaction_hash (ignored). Source referenced via Etherscan token page.
experiment_input: Source: Etherscan MCO2 token page (https://etherscan.io/token/0xfC98e825A2264D890F9a1e68ed50E1526abCcacD). Size: not explicitly stated (number of transactions/rows not provided). Preprocessing: block_number retained as numerical (no scaling), timestamp encoded as cyclical sine/cosine, from_address/to_address/token_name/token_symbol label-encoded, transaction_hash ignored, token_value and gas_price robust-scaled to mitigate outliers. Focused subset involving ten major nodes.
experiment_process: 1) Preprocess raw blockchain records as above. 2) Two quantum feature extraction strategies: (a) Random QF: instantiate untrained/random parameter QNNs to generate parameters for a classical NN and extract features (Monte Carlo runs reported as worst/average/best); (b) Fully trained QNN: train QNN end-to-end with SwAV loss (Algorithm 1) across varying num_prototypes and quantum_depth, using Adam optimizer and gradient clipping. Within each training batch, compute QNN outputs, create two augmented views by adding Gaussian noise N(0,σ^2), compute SwAV loss between views, backpropagate, and update parameters. After training, run QNN in evaluation mode to extract quantum features per batch (no grad). 3) Concatenate quantum features with preprocessed classical features to form hybrid representations. 4) Apply K-Means clustering for K in {2,3,4,5,6}. 5) Evaluate clusters using Silhouette Score, Davies-Bouldin Index, and Calinski-Harabasz Index to select candidate K values. 6) Feed cluster outputs into an AI Agent pipeline: re-encode hashed values, build hierarchical Clustered Information Base (depths, epochs, clusters), run Cluster Meaning Generation for each cluster, perform intra-epoch summarization, inter-strategy comparisons (QNN vs QF), and store cluster-, epoch-, and strategy-level insights in the Knowledge Base. 7) Synthesize final recommendations (quantitative + qualitative), with convergence on K=3.
experiment_output: Quantitative outputs: internal clustering metrics per run and configuration — Silhouette Score, Davies-Bouldin Index, Calinski-Harabasz Index; comparisons of QF (worst/average/best Monte Carlo runs) vs QNN across K=2..6 (tables of metric values reported). Qualitative outputs: LLM-generated semantic cluster descriptions, identification of singleton/high-value clusters in QNN, broader token/interaction-pattern clusters in QF, intra- and inter-strategy summaries, and a final recommendation (ensemble/hybridization potential and endorsement of K=3). Baselines: Monte Carlo untrained QF runs and classical baselines implied but not numerically detailed.

results_summary: The paper introduces a hybrid two-stage pipeline combining internal metric-driven clustering evaluation with an LLM-powered AI Agent for qualitative interpretation on an Ethereum MCO2 transaction dataset. Two quantum-enhanced feature strategies were compared: Monte Carlo Random Quantum Features (QF) and fully trained Quantum Neural Networks (QNN) trained with a SwAV loss. Using K-means and internal metrics (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz), the authors report that trained QNNs consistently achieve superior internal clustering scores versus QF runs. The AI Agent produced semantic cluster descriptions that revealed QNN often isolates high-value/singleton clusters (useful for anomaly detection) while QF captures broader token and relational patterns. Quantitative and qualitative analyses in the paper both favor K=3 for this dataset, and the authors argue for the complementary use of QNN and QF and future autonomous, AI-driven clustering refinement.

Quantum Features (QF) best runs in Table 3 report Silhouette Scores exceeding 0.99 in some runs and Calinski-Harabasz indices up to the order of 1e12; worst/average QF runs have much lower Silhouette Scores (~0.31–0.66) and Davies-Bouldin in the ~0.4–1.05 range.
Both QF and QNN experiments (quantitative + AI Agent) converge on K=3 as the preferred cluster configuration for the studied dataset.

Therefore the assertion remains suggestive/speculative rather than definitively demonstrated.
